The future of the Piedmont Community Pool will be up to the voters this fall in the form of a bond measure that would redesign the facility. On November 3, Piedmonters will vote to either support or reject a bond issue initially pegged at $19 million. Numerous City Council and Recreation Commission meetings have alerted the public of ongoing, long-term issues with the aquatic facility, including an outer-shell leak causing a loss of 1,000 gallons of water a day. At each digital meeting, calls poured in from concerned residents over the future of the city’s only public pool (the school district has none). The majority of callers supported the decision to place a bond on this year’s ballot, and showed interest in a redesign of the facility. This is not the first time that a redesign has been offered for the 56-year-old pool. It originally opened in 1964 and has had no major renovations. articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council on July 24. Editor: I want to compliment you on the great jobs you are doing for our city under very trying circumstances. I imagine you never ever thought that your jobs would involve working during a Pandemic. Please accept my sincere thanks. I do have some very serious concerns about REACH rules and regulations proposed to be instituted within our city building code. Of course, I am speaking about my own situation, but I would guess that there are many others in the same boat. My husband and I are in our twilight years (81 and 78) and living on a fixed income. We also live in a home that is about to be 100 years old. We have lived in it for 48 years. Our home has a tile roof as well as a boiler/circulating hot water system that is powered by natural gas. Should I be required to change out that heating system, it would be a tremendous financial burden and may not even be possible without remodeling every room in the house and cost many thousands of dollars. Likewise, if I wanted to do a roof repair and was told that I had to add solar, it would be extremely complicated and costly. I might choose to take all the tile off and put on a composition roof that would make for a change that would ruin the character of the house. I can see this happening to a lot of homeowners who have been in Piedmont in older homes for many years. At this point in our lives, we want to stay in Piedmont and do the best we can with repairs and not be forced to leave because of REACH. I would like to suggest that for these older homes and older people, REACH would only be triggered by the sale of the house. This would allow the seller and buyer to negotiate upon whom the financial burden would fall. I would hate these REACH rules to be the factor that forced people to leave our beautiful city. In my case, that would mean leaving a city that has been my home for 78 years. I believe that there are many similarly situated homeowners who are not aware of what you are proposing, and if they knew, they would be outraged. Please consider the above as you make your decisions about REACH. Thank you, –Fran Wolfe
articles.title: REACH codes have big impact on older homes

articles.text: Staff photo After making an appointment, Piedmont resident Lee Alering (left) was able to drive to the Carriage House and leave donations with Dress Best for Less with DBFL employee Sharon Sanford. Dress Best for Less, the community’s thrift shop, is now accepting donations at the Carriage House at 799 Magnolia Avenue, but by appointment only. Its retail shop next to Piedmont Grocery at 4020 Piedmont Avenue has been open since June 17, but it does bit have adequate storage space for accepting donations. The Carriage House, which houses a sorting and marking room for the store, recently received clearance to accept donations by appointment. Appointments to donate must be made at www.dressbestforless.org. DBFL can no longer sell directly out of the Carriage House. It will be used for drive-up donations and sorting only. Sales will occur at its store on Piedmont Avenue, but only higher end goods can be accepted. Recommended items for donation include nearly new: women’s summer tops, handbags, purses, jewelry, men’s tops, home decor, kid’s clothes, toys & puzzles, books, designer items, and even ski and snowboard apparel. Many people have backlogs of “pandemic spring cleaning” donations in wait, but patience will be required. “If we opened up to regular donations in our bin out front, we would get dumped on again,” said DBFL chair Linda Smith Munyan, noting the double function of donations by appointment only. “It gives the store a chance to re-educate our donors. People have been used to giving us everything. It’s more effective to explain this in a conversation vs. signs on the building,” she said. Dress Best for Less has experienced slow sales since its reopening, around 50 percent of normal. Much of their proceeds benefit Piedmont schools. On Thursday July 30, appointments are available from 9-12. Future schedules will be be Tuesdays and Wednesdays from 9-12 and Saturdays from 10-1. Everyone must wear a mask and adhere to social distancing.

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation recently announced that Colleen Allan, Amelie Kappes, and Teebie Saunders will be co-chairs of this year’s Giving Campaign for Piedmont schools. They will lead the community-wide effort to raise $3 million to keep Piedmont schools strong. “Every school year it costs the Piedmont Unified School District roughly $18,000 to educate each student in Piedmont. Federal, state, and local funding pays for all but $1,700-2,000 per child of that amount,” said Kappes. “As a community, we are responsible for closing this gap, and each year Piedmont has stepped up and shown we are committed to doing this.” The three chairs have been working throughout the summer to prepare for a campaign kickoff on September 1. An extensive committee of parents representing Piedmont’s six schools is also on board to amplify the outreach of the campaign. For more information on the Piedmont Education Foundation and its annual Giving Campaign, visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org. The Fremont Bank Way.

Meg Adler, illustrator of Outside the Lines: A Coloring Book for Rebels. Meg Adler, a Piedmont High School alum, recently published a coloring book with a Bay Area collaborative focus. Adler was born and raised in Piedmont, and her parents, Wayne and Melissa Batavia, still live in the same house in which she grew up. She is a proud alum of Wildwood elementary, Piedmont Middle School, and Piedmont High School. Her interest in art started when she was a young girl, but other than taking a semester of art in high school, she is primarily selftaught. She drew inspiration from her grandmother’s calligraphy. Adler said that her real interest in art as a career came through art therapy, when she was 12 years old. own marks. There’s little prompts throughout,” Adler said. A big aspect of the book, she said, is that it challenges the artist to think outside the norm. “A big part of my art is to think creatively, and to try and represent that,” Adler said. Adler owns a small illustration business called Letters, Aligned. She started the business in 2014. Materials: • Pencil or Pen • Scissors • Tape or Glue • Markers or Crayons (to decorate) • Reusable Materials: • Cardboard • Construction Paper • Paper cups • Toothpicks • Foil • Straws • Pipe Cleaners • Popsicle Sticks • Egg Cartons • Toilet Paper or Paper Towel Procedure: 1. Build the body of your rover. You can use a variety of materials for the body, but it should be something sturdy that you can attach other materials to. 2. Decorate the base. You can paint, color, or wrap your body however you’d like. 3. Build the wheels and legs of your rover. For help making a rover that rolls, follow steps (4-9) below. Materials that are round and can roll make great wheels. Straws are a helpful material if you’d like to build a rover that rolls. 4. Tape a straw, or cylinder of paper horizontally across the bottom of your rover. 5. Repeat with one, two, or three more straws/paper cylinders. Try to make them equally spaced out on your rover. 6. Identify the materials you will be using as wheels, and as axles. The axel will hold your two wheels together. You will need the same number of axles as paper cylinders or straws, and twice the number of wheels. 7. Thread your axle material through the straws or paper cylinders underneath your rover. 8. Use tape or glue to attach the center of your wheel to one end of an axle. Make sure the axel is still threaded through the straws on your rover! 9. Repeat so that each axle has two wheels attached to it and is suspending on the bottom of your rover. 10. Add the arms, neck, and head to your rover. Use glue, tape, or poke them through the body of your rover to hold them in place. Strong, skinny materials that can stand up make good arms or necks. Get creative and add different tools to the ends of your rover arms, too. 11. Add a brain, and an energy source to your rover. You can make them out of paper, cardboard, or whatever material you think works best. 12. Add logos, a flag, even passengers to your rover. 13. Encourage others to build their own rover, too. They can even use different materials than you to build their rover. Find more activities and at-home experiments on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. articles.text: City alleges new FCC rules would further limit local control of cell towers T h e P i e d m o n t Pl a n - ning Department released an announcement on Tuesday, July 21 outlining its opposition to new guidelines recently passed by the Federal Communications Commission that limit how local governments can regulate cell towers. “We believe there are ways for wireless communication devices to be deployed in an aesthetically appropriate manner,” Kevin Jackson, the Director of Planning and Building, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, the FCC seems intent on making that much more difficult, if not impossible.” The announcement came one day after Piedmont City Council voted to join a coalition of cities opposing the rules. On June 9, the FCC adopted a new ruling that altered how municipalities handle permits for wireless facilities. Specifically, the FCC modified Section 6409(a) of the Spectrum Act of 2012. The section requires cities like Piedmont to approve requests from wireless infrastructure companies to modify existing wireless towers and base stations if the physical dimensions do not undergo a “substantially change.” The new decision alters the meaning of “substantial change.” As long as a wireless infrastructure company follows FCC rules, cities cannot deny height or size increases of existing cell antennae even if the modifications would violate aesthetic conditions, such as vegetation screening or fencing requirements, that were initially imposed when the antennae were first approved. The FCC now allows antenna to be up to 20 feet tall and there is no height maximum for new antennae built outside the public right-of-way. Furthermore, the FCC allows that wireless infrastructure companies can install more equipment cabinets per request to make modifications to existing structures. The FCC also changed the definition of “concealment” in regard to wireless facility building requests so that concealment only means “stealth” design, meaning a cell tower that is meant to look like something else, like a tree. Under the order, cities requesting concealment of cell towers could not require screening by a rooftop or tree line. Additionally, timing requirements were altered by the FCC as part of the rule change. Cities must make decisions on wireless facility application within a standardized 60-day “shot clock” period. The new rules mean that the “shot clock” period starts earlier in the application process, when the applicants start the first procedural steps of submitting a proposal. This tightened timeline gives cities less opportunity to publicize and have public discussions about the applications. In response, Piedmont joined a coalition of cities, organized by law firm Best Best & Krieger (BBK), in opposition to the new FCC rules. Comments against the rule change must be filed by August 10. “Unless there is a court-ordered injunction, the new FCC rules will further reduce Piedmont’s ability to control the installation of wireless communication facilities,” Jackson continued. The action is the latest volley between Piedmont and the FCC over cell tower regulations, especially since Ajit Pai was appointed Chairman of the commission by President Trump in 2017. Publicly, the cell tower issue has been a major point of controversy in Piedmont for more than three years. In late 2016, wireless infrastructure builder Crown Castle submitted plans to build several small cell antennas around the City. After years of protest and legal battles, Council approved several of plans from the company last year as part of a settlement with Crown Castle. In 2018 and 2019, the Council agreed to join organized coalitions in opposed to new FCC rules that make it harder for cities to regulate cell towers. articles.text: In collaboration with the Oakland League of Women Voters (LWVP), the Piedmont League of Women Voters presented Part 2 of “New Models for Social Justice – Police Reform” on Monday, July 20 with guest speaker Anne Janks, Organizer at the Coalition for Police Accountability. Janks, a resident of Oakland for 25 years, has worked as a union organizer under varied labor laws. She has spent time with workers’ rights education, legislative campaigns, fundraising, website development, and social media advocacy. She began volunteering with the Coalition for Police Accountability in 2016 during the campaign for a ballot measure to create an independent community body to oversee the Oakland Police Department. The resulting Oakland Police Commission is the strongest independent oversight body in the country, with authority to write policy, independently investigate and discipline officers, and fire the police chief. Janks was introduced by LWVP member Lois Corrin. Janks described her involvement with the independent oversight body. In the midst of their campaign in 2016, the Oakland Police Department made national headlines, chronicling some Oakland officers’ involvements in trafficking an underage female. “It had the collateral effect of ensuring that we ended up with the strongest oversight body of a police agency anywhere in the country,” Janks said. One of the largest capabilities of the citizen-led commission is the ability to hire and fire officers and the police chief, which was demonstrated earlier this year. Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf fired former Oakland Police Chief Anne Kirkpatrick, acting on the recommendation of the Oakland Police Commission. “The only challenge about having the commission is that there is an ongoing struggle for resources and independence. There are certainly [citizens] within the city who want to undermine [the commission’s] ability to function independently,” Janks said. Janks then described anecdotes that she said proved a need for police reform and accountability. “There was an instance [in 2018] where our police officers had been called to a scene where a man was sleeping in between two houses, and there was a gun nearby. Over about 40 minutes, they couldn’t come up with a plan with what to do,” Janks said. The result in that encounter, Janks said, was that officers tried to wake up the man who became agitated, and then was shot to death by an officer. “Ad vo c a t e s f r o m t h e un-housed community who had known [the man] came to say they didn’t understand why this would happen,” she said. The result was an organized hearing on policing in the homeless community. It became overwhelming clear, Janks said, that most interactions between homeless community members and Oakland police officers were negative. MACRO, or mobile assistance community responders of Oakland, is a pilot program formed to combat social issues that may be better handled by community members than police officers. The pilot program is heralded by the Coalition for Police Accountability, which began pushing for the city to adopt a MACRO-like program since early 2019. Although nationwide calls for defunding the police have now become commonplace, the pilot program is really the product of years of grassroots research and advocacy, Janks said. “The structure of the pilot is that we will use people from the community as much as possible. Counselors will have some combination of doing similar outreach work, and provided training,” Janks said. After her presentation, Janks answered questions from viewers. You can watch the presentation on Yout ube at ht t p s://w w w.yout u b e.c om / watch?v=9oFnOxpP5zU. This was the second part of a two-part series on police reform hosted by the LWVP. Part one featured Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and Deputy Attorney General Nancy Beninati.

pages.text: Wednesday, July 29, 2020 9 League of Women Voters hosts New Models for Social Justice: Police Reform, Part 2 By Allyson Aleksey In collaboration with the Oakland League of Women Voters (LWVP), the Piedmont League of Women Voters presented Part 2 of “New Models for Social Justice – Police Reform” on Monday, July 20 with guest speaker Anne Janks, Organizer at the Coalition for Police Accountability. Janks, a resident of Oakland for 25 years, has worked as a union organizer under varied labor laws. She has spent time with workers’ rights education, legislative campaigns, fundraising, website development, and social media advocacy. She began volunteering with the Coalition for Police Accountability in 2016 during the campaign for a ballot measure to create an independent community body to oversee the Oakland Police Department. The resulting Oakland Police Commission is the strongest independent oversight body in the country, with authority to write policy, independently investigate and discipline officers, and fire the police chief. Janks was introduced by LWVP member Lois Corrin. Janks described her involvement with the independent oversight body. In the midst of their campaign in 2016, the Oakland Police Department made national headlines, chronicling some Oakland officers’ involvements in trafficking an underage female. “It had the collateral effect of ensuring that we ended up with the strongest oversight body of a police agency anywhere in the country,” Janks said. One of the largest capabilities of the citizen-led commission is the ability to hire and fire officers and the police chief, which was demonstrated earlier this year. Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf fired former Oakland Police Chief Anne Kirkpatrick, acting on the recommendation of the Oakland Police Commission. “The only challenge about having the commission is that there is an ongoing struggle for resources and independence. There are certainly [citizens] within the city who want to undermine [the commission’s] ability to function independently,” Janks said. Janks then described anecdotes that she said proved a need for police reform and accountability. “There was an instance [in 2018] where our police officers had been called to a scene where a man was sleeping in between two houses, and there was a gun nearby. Over about 40 minutes, they couldn’t come up with a plan with what to do,” Janks said. The result in that encounter, Janks said, was that officers tried to wake up the man who became agitated, and then was shot to death by an officer. “Ad vo c a t e s f r o m t h e un-housed community who had known [the man] came to say they didn’t understand why this would happen,” she said. The result was an organized hearing on policing in the homeless community. It became overwhelming clear, Janks said, that most interactions between homeless community members and Oakland police officers were negative. MACRO, or mobile assistance community responders of Oakland, is a pilot program formed to combat social issues that may be better handled by community members than police officers. The pilot program is heralded by the Coalition for Police Accountability, which began pushing for the city to adopt a MACRO-like program since early 2019. Although nationwide calls for defunding the police have now become commonplace, the pilot program is really the product of years of grassroots research and advocacy, Janks said. “The structure of the pilot is that we will use people from the community as much as possible. Counselors will have some combination of doing similar outreach work, and provided training,” Janks said. After her presentation, Janks answered questions from viewers. You can watch the presentation on Yout ube at ht t p s://w w w.yout u b e.c om / watch?v=9oFnOxpP5zU. This was the second part of a two-part series on police reform hosted by the LWVP. Part one featured Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and Deputy Attorney General Nancy Beninati. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Scott Hill A team photo of the 1976 Piedmont football team, the only football team to win a NCS title. Last week, we published an article regarding Piedmont’s only football team to win the North Coast Section championship. With apologies, it contained a number of factual errors. The year was 1976, and legendary coach Bob Muenter had retired after 25 years as head coach to become the school’s Athletic Director, a position he held until 1983. Kevin McNair was named head coach of the powerhouse football program, and with Clark Ransom as his Defensive Coordinator, they became the best football team in the area, bar none. McNair’s team was undefeated and won the league title. It went on to win the North Coast Section championship in a two-game format, a 20-8 win over Salesian in the finals after defeating Sunset high of Hayward 14-7 in the semi-finals. Sunset closed its doors as a school in 1990. Piedmont’s Mike Humphries, for whom the current baseball field is named, was a scout coach for the football team in 1976. He recently described McNair as one of the most fiery coaches he has known. “He was so intense it was unbelievable,” said Humphries. “He had this red face that would just get redder; he looked like he was going to blow up. There’d be moments where Clark would have to call some offensive plays because Kevin had gotten so emotional,” he added. McNair, who also coached track & field at Piedmont, went on to coach Occidental College’s track and field program, and Ransom turned his focus on a career in real estate. Jeff Dreher, the namesake of the football teams perpetual Offensive Lineman award, was part of the team, as was Sports Hall of Fame fullback and linebacker Jeff Haile, then the league’s Player of the Year. Haile was also an All-League track and field athlete in shotput and to this day holds the school’s record in the event. He went on to play football and rugby for Stanford and was elected to the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2014. With video footage discovered on YouTube, you can witness Haile barreling through the line in games against Encinal, San Leandro, Miramonte, and Albany, as the Highlanders beat Sunset at Pacific Field in San Leandro, now Burrell Field. Humphries said the 20-8 championship win over Salesian came on a blustery night late that fall. “It was a stormy night with big winds,” he recalled. “In the fourth quarter, Salesian had the wind at their face, and we knew then we would win. I’ll never forget coming back to Piedmont on the bus and the lights were out in Oakland and tree limbs were down everywhere. It was a wild and crazy night.” Those Piedmont years were characterized by its stout defense and aggressive linemen, featuring Seth Bobbitt, Ken Chan, Scott Guel, and Kent Jordan, who briefly signed with the Raiders. Peter Craig was a running back, pairing in the backfield with Haile. Bob Brueckner was quarterback, and David Loomis the receiver. Watching the film of that team you can witness some Piedmont supporters in the small visiting stands with signs reading “Upset Sunset,” and classic cars along the fence line. After Piedmont’s only NCS championship, it took five years before they got to the semifinals, losing to 28-14 to San Lorenzo. Piedmont didn’t reach the NCS semifinals again until Scott Coats coached the 2014 program to a school-record 12-1 season and a WACC league title. Seeded No. 2, Piedmont was upset by No. 3 Justin-Siena 14-3 in the semi-finals. The 2016 team under James Holan also advanced to the NCS semi-finals, but lost to No. 1 Cardinal Newman.

articles.text: Photo by Robert Davis Nikolai Littleton set Piedmont High’s single season scoring record with 49 goals back in 2010. With the Premier League now over and Champions and Europa League on the docket, we take a look back to one of the Piedmont High boys’ all-time bests performances, the senior years of soccer player Nikolai Littleton, who set a school record with 49 goals. It was 10 years ago, and Piedmont High was coming off hallmark Bay Shore Athletic League championship seasons in 2007 and 2008 under coach Peter Hayton during Littleton’s freshman and sophomore years – both undefeated seasons. In 2009, Marques Dillard was hired to lead the team and coached them to another Bay Shore championship and Division 2 North Coast Section semifinals berth. At that time, NCS had only two soccer brackets. It’s now up to four with PHS in the smallschool Div. 4 bracket. Littleton and the team lit up scoreboards that season with a bundle of impressive shutouts and one-sided victories, including: 4-0 and 5-1 wins on St. Patrick, 9-0 and 10-2 against St. Joseph, 7-0 vs. Swett, and 4-0 against both Salesian and Encinal. Litttleton set a school record with the number of games in which he scored three goals. He closed his career at Witter Field with two goals against El Cerrito in the opening round of the NCS playoffs. The team was 12-3-1 in league and 16-5-3 overall. Littleton received a first-team All-League selection and briefly went on to play overseas in the U.K. before returning home. He’s now a wingback on the Oakland Roots pro soccer club and earned starting minutes before the season was shut down due to the coronavirus. “Littleton’s 49 goals led the East Bay. Albany’s Gabriel Borges was a distant second with 26 goals,” wrote the Post’s James Bucci in 2010. Also, on that team was Christian Smit, who received a firstteam all-league selection as a junior, and defender Ralston Louie with second-team honors. It seems that in 2010 with Littleton’s scoring record and departure from the school, the stature of the Piedmont boys’ program went with him. In the years to follow, there have been a number of coaches, including Rory O’Connor from 2012 until Todd Sullivan’s hire in 2016. Sullivan wound up hiring Littleton as his assistant coach at PHS, a decision that led to huge dividends. Coming full circle, Sullivan, Littleton, and the 2019 team won the school’s first league title since 2009 after going 9-0-1 in the Shoreline Division of the WACC. By Jonathan Comeaux Last week, we published an article regarding Piedmont’s only football team to win the North Coast Section championship. With apologies, it contained a number of factual errors. The year was 1976, and legendary coach Bob Muenter had retired after 25 years as head coach to become the school’s Athletic Director, a position he held until 1983. Kevin McNair was named head coach of the powerhouse football program, and with Clark Ransom as his Defensive Coordinator, they became the best football team in the area, bar none. McNair’s team was undefeated and won the league title. It went on to win the North Coast Section championship in a two-game format, a 20-8 win over Salesian in the finals after defeating Sunset high of Hayward 14-7 in the semi-finals. Sunset closed its doors as a school in 1990. Piedmont’s Mike Humphries, for whom the current baseball field is named, was a scout coach for the football team in 1976. He recently described McNair as one of the most fiery coaches he has known. “He was so intense it was unbelievable,” said Humphries. “He had this red face that would just get redder; he looked like he was going to blow up. There’d be moments where Clark would have to call some offensive plays because Kevin had gotten so emotional,” he added. McNair, who also coached track & field at Piedmont, went on to coach Occidental College’s track and field program, and Ransom turned his focus on a career in real estate. Haile was also an All-League track and field athlete in shotput and to this day holds the school’s record in the event. He went on to play football and rugby for Stanford and was elected to the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2014. With video footage discovered on YouTube, you can witness Haile barreling through the line in games against Encinal, San Leandro, Miramonte, and Albany, as the Highlanders beat Sunset at Pacific Field in San Leandro, now Burrell Field. Humphries said the 20-8 championship win over Salesian came on a blustery night late that fall. “It was a stormy night with big winds,” he recalled. “In the fourth quarter, Salesian had the wind at their face, and we knew then we would win. I’ll never forget coming back to Piedmont on the bus and the lights were out in Oakland and tree limbs were down everywhere. It was a wild and crazy night.” Those Piedmont years were characterized by its stout defense and aggressive linemen, featuring Seth Bobbitt, Ken Chan, Scott Guel, and Kent Jordan, who briefly signed with the Raiders. Peter Craig was a running back, pairing in the backfield with Haile. Bob Brueckner was quarterback, and David Loomis the receiver. Watching the film of that team you can witness some Piedmont supporters in the small visiting stands with signs reading “Upset Sunset,” and classic cars along the fence line. After Piedmont’s only NCS championship, it took five years before they got to the semifinals, losing to 28-14 to San Lorenzo. Piedmont didn’t reach the NCS semifinals again until Scott Coats coached the 2014 program to a school-record 12-1 season and a WACC league title. Seeded No. 2, Piedmont was upset by No. 3 Justin-Siena 14-3 in the semi-finals. The 2016 team under James Holan also advanced to the NCS semi-finals, but lost to No. 1 Cardinal Newman. articles.text: The 38th and final Premier League game was played on Championship Sunday, July 26, finalizing qualification for Champions League and Europa League by way of the table. But Monday, July 13’s ruling of Manchester City winning their appeal against UEFA’s two year ban from UEFA games (Champions and Europa) was perhaps the biggest news. It also reduces their $32.5 million fine to $11 million and notes no wrongdoing of Financial Fair Play rules, which are cost controls to mitigate the gap between bigger and smaller clubs. Back in February, UEFA ruled that City committed multiple violations related to club licensing by overstating its sponsorship revenue and break-even information from 2012-2016, while the organization failed to cooperate in the investigation. City’s ownership, the City Football Group, and the Court of Arbitrations cited that UEFA’s own rules prevent them from handing an immediate ban against their organization due to a five-year time limit for breach of Financial Fair Play rules, effectively barring an official investigation. It’s a massive win for City on a technicality. Some around the league, like Tottenham manager Jose Mourinho, had harsh words about the ruling: “If they are guilty, they should be banned. In any case, the decision is a disaster. If you are not guilty, you should not pay [an $11 million fine]. I am not saying Man. City is not guilty. I know money for them is easy, but it’s a principle. Even a pound. Why are you paying eight, nine million? It is a disgrace,” said Mourinho in his naturally brash style. Photo courtesy of Manchestercity.com Manchester City and manager Pep Guardiola have won their appeal against UEFA’s two-year ban from Champions League and Europa League. Final Table The Manchester City ruling means that the usual top-four in the Premier League table qualified for Champions League: Liverpool (99 points), City (81 points), Manchester United (66 points) and Chelsea (66 points). The Red Devils, as expected, catapulted above Leicester City (62 points) for a Champions League spot by defeating them 2-0 on Sunday, sending the Foxes down to a fifth place Europa League qualification spot. The difference between Champions League and Europa, you ask? Around €60 million from prize money alone; a max earning from UCL scored 2019 champions Liverpool €82.45 million. From UEL, Chelsea earned €21.34 million. With TV deals, advertising revenue, and ticket sales for Champions League added in there, the difference between the two is closer to €100 million. But for 2019 UCL runner up Tottenham (59 points), pushing into Europa with the sixth spot on the table should be taken as a huge win. They overtook the Wolves of Wolverhampton, who also finished with 59 points but had a worse goal differential with a 2-0 loss to Chelsea on Sunday. Their 1-1 draw with Crystal Palace was enough to get the job done for the Hotspur and new manager Mourinho, who took over the job in November from former manager Mauricio Pochettino with Tottenham near bottom of the table in 14th. Hotspur’s North London counterpart Arsenal did itself no favors on Tuesday, July 21 with a 1-0 loss to Aston Villa. The Gunners finished 8th, out of a Europa qualification spot and lowest it’s finished on the table in 25 years. But their hopes are not all forgotten. Arsenal and Chelsea square off in a London Derby for the FA Cup Trophy, which would automatically qualify the Gunners for Europa. As for Chelsea, they got bigger fish to fry. Champions and Europa League Finales With the Premier League gone, we’re onto the European tour of Champions and Europa League—where the top teams from England, Italy, Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, and even Greece, Turkey, Croatia, and Russia compete. Both leagues finished on the second leg’s games in the Round of 16. UCL returns Friday, August 7 with Cristiano Ronaldo, Paulo Dybala, and Juventus fighting from a 1-0 deficit against Lyon of France. Manchester City currently holds a 2-1 aggregate advantage over Real Madrid, where superstar Sergio Ramos will be unavailable due to a Red Card received on February 26’s first leg. Chelsea also plays German giant, Bayern Munich. Leo Messi and Barcelona are drawn 1-1 with Italy’s Napoli. UEL is back sooner on August 5, Manchester United are the hands-down favorites, up 5-0 over LASK of Austria from the first leg. Inter Milan of Serie A’s Italian league and the Wolves are two more teams to keep an eye on. The winner of Europa gets automatic qualification to next year’s Champions League. 14 Wednesday, July 29, 2020 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 13th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. WALTER TEITELBAUM Cross Country & Track Eduardo Calvo-Salinas, PHS Class of 2017, transferred from the University of Portland to Seattle Pacific University and is their starting midfielder. EDUARDO CALVO-SALINAS Soccer Piedmont High Class of 2017 Seattle Pacific University Class of 2021 Eduardo Calvo-Salinas joined the University of Portland’s Div. 1 soccer program coming out of Piedmont High in 2017 but transferred to Seattle Pacific University in 2019 as a sophomore and quickly entered the starting lineup as a midfielder. In 2019, Calvo-Salinas appeared in 16 games and started 12, scoring one goal and two assists while logging 1,170 minutes on the pitch. During his senior year at PHS, he earned first-team All-League honors for the 2016-2017 season under then first-year head coach Todd Sullivan and was the team’s leading scorer as a midfielder. What is your workout program this summer? I’ve made sure to stay fit by doing different types of workouts every day. My workouts include: - 5-8 mile runs to keep my cardio and fitness levels up. - Lifting weights for upper and lower body strength and other core, full body routines. - Doing technical drills to make sure my touch stays sharp. - Using the stationary bike at home, or going on rides with the mountain bike. I’ve also been playing pickup soccer at Stanford with some talented college players from around the area; even a couple of professional players joined us as well. What are your fitness goals for the summer? To stay as fit and sharp as possible while staying healthy to prevent any sort of injury. Lastly, I have been paying close attention to my nutrition and have been eating very healthy since the start of the pandemic. Nutrition is very important and can definitely help avoid injuries and boost performance. How are you measuring your development? By timing all of my runs and workouts. I am also gradually increasing the amount of weight I lift, the amount of distance I run, and the amount of time that my workouts last. I’ve also been tracking my sleep patterns and how that relates to my performance. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? On my own and with other college soccer players from around the area. However, I normally train with Nikolai Littleton, who I believe is the best certified trainer in the Bay Area and a talented wingback on the Oakland Roots pro team. He has helped my development tremendously ever since I got to Piedmont in 2014. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Being able to maintain consistent workouts every day since late-March. I’ve managed to stay fit and sharp throughout this whole process as a result of completing these daily routines while also being able to take care of my online summer courses, schoolwork, and work. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Never stop working on your crafts, to not make any excuses, to work extremely hard, be disciplined, fight for their dreams and goals, and always stay true to themselves. Hard work pays off. In these difficult times, it is important to stay positive and always believe in yourself. Walter Teitelbaum, PHS Class of 2018, is entering his junior year on the UC Santa Cruz cross country and track programs. He hopes to help the Banana Slugs reach the NCAA Div.3 National Championships for a secondconsecutive season. Piedmont High Class of 2018 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2022 Walter Teitelbaum graduated from Piedmont High in 2018 and is currently running for the UC Santa Cruz cross country and track programs, embarking on his junior campaign this fall. Teitelbaum was among his team’s top finishers in the 2019 Division III NCAA West Region Cross Country Championship, helping his school finished 3rd. He also competed with the Banana Slugs in the Division III NCAA Cross County Championships. He graduated from Piedmont High in 2018. He earned a firstteam All-League selection in 2017 after helping lead the PHS cross-country team to a berth in the State Championship. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I moved to Boulder, Colorado with my friend so I could train at altitude to improve my overall fitness while taking summer classes online because of the virus. My summer training has mostly been the following: Monday: Rest day or an easier 30-50 min run. Tuesday: 10min warmup jog; drills and speed development; 40-65 min training run Wednesday: Pre-Meet (20min jog, drills, strides); Aerobic Tempo (4-8 miles depending on assigned pace; Cooldown, 15-30min shakeout later in the day. Thursday: Mid-Week Long Run (60-80min). Friday: Pre-Meet (20min jog, drills, strides); 10-30 min Cooldown Saturday: Either Progression, 50-60 min cutting down every mile to about 5:30, or just a 50-75 min training run. Sunday: Long run day, 80-100 min. What are your fitness goals for this summer? This summer training plan has allowed me to do the work that I feel like my body can handle without feeling too tired in order to avoid the long term effects of burning out from overtraining. This summer I am gradually working up to about 70 miles per week, last summer I was at about 60, and the summer before that, 50. I am very proud of the success I have had by doing consistent summer running and I feel like it has made the biggest impact on my running ability as well as injury prevention. How are you measuring your development? By timing my results and measuring my weekly progress and energy output. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out on my own with athletic instruction and workouts from my coaches, David Klech and Shawn Gallup. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I was able to help score for my team all season and qualify us for the West Regional XC Championship, where I placed top 35 and earned all-region awards. We also reached the National XC Championship, where our men’s program placed 22nd overall. This last track season, as short as it was, I was able to run 15:30 in the 5k, 8:30 in the 3k, and 4:04 in the 1500m, way better than I ever would’ve imagined when in high school. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? My advice for anyone who is interested in getting into running would be to set goals for yourself and make it a habit to go out and run in the morning, despite how hard it is. Running is an accumulation of experience as well as fitness, and although it can take months or even years to see improvement, it becomes worth it when you realize the organization that it can bring to your life and the friends you will make along the way. For a high schooler who might be interested in running competitively in college, I couldn’t recommend choosing a Division III school more. Running at a D3 level has allowed me to continue to focus on my school and learning as my first priority without any compromise to my running. My teammates and coaches are my favorite humans on the planet and they help in all aspects of college life, whether it’s doing schoolwork, getting good sleep, eating right, or making the right decisions (things that are very difficult to do in college these days). BEN LEVINSON Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2021 Ben Levinson is set to enter his senior year and has the potential to be among the baseball team’s strongest arms on the mound and a strong hitter. The Highlanders were 3-2 prior to the stoppage of play this spring Levinson was 1-1 with a team-leading nine strikeouts as a starting pitcher. As a batter, he carried a .400 average with six hits, four RBIs, and three runs scored. Levinson was named an Honorable Mention player of the year by the Post in his sophomore year in 2019 after he went 6-1 with 36 strikeouts in 49 innings of work and opened the season with a no-hitter against Head-Royce. What is your workout program this summer? I’ve been given workout plans from my brothers [Owen and Nate Levinson], who both play college baseball, and also getting instruction from coaches. For pitching, it’s really important to have strong legs so I’ve been focusing on strengthening my lower body. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goal is just to get stronger. Throwing harder will help pitching at the next level. How are you measuring your development? I’ve been throwing a lot of bullpens recently and tracking my velocity. I’ve been able to steadily increase my velocity, which is a good sign. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’ve mostly been working on my own but also work with pitching coach Steve Thobe, who has also helped me to get stronger and develop more as a pitcher. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Recently, I recorded my highest pitching velocity. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Find time whenever you can to put in work, whether that’s lifting weights, or skill-work for a specific sport. As you reach higher levels, the competition only gets harder. If you don’t work hard and aren’t motivated to get better in any way that you can, you might not get as far and be able to play as much as you would want to. Ben Levinson is entering his senior year at Piedmont High. After his junior year was canceled due to the coronavirus, Levinson has his eyes set on a big senior campaign.

articles.text: For this week’s outdoors series, we’re heading out over the water on the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge to grab some sweeping views of the Bay We start at the entrance at Tewksbury Avenue near Point Richmond and travel 5.5 miles across the Richmond Bridge to Point San Quentin, a nice 11-mile round trip. Guidelines for hiking amidst the coronavirus include: • Start with research parking or trail restrictions. Plan your route. • Be mindful. Always bring a face cover of some sort. • The earlier the better. Trails are most trafficked past noon. • No large groups. The bike and pedestrian path opened in November of 2019 and to my surprise isn’t as popular as one would imagine. On a Friday at noon, I saw just seven bikers throughout the day, meaning I would go miles without passing another person. There were no groups, and just one man with his daughter and a few fishermen hanging around Point San Quentin. The path on the Richmond Bridge is 10-feet wide, giving ample space for hikers and bikers. The trail is not as developed as the similar Bay Bridge Trail, which has a guard rail and fair amount of space separating you from traffic. On the Richmond Bridge it’s just you, concrete barriers, and cars zooming by on I-80. get increasingly better views of Point Molate and Point San Pablo toward the peak of the Richmond Bridge. You’ll also get a glimpse of the tiny Red Rock Island on your way into Marin County. elevation reading of 920 feet, but the ascent was easily manageable. This trek would be good for the beginning level hiker, child, or for cyclists working on their sprints. cisco Bay Trail for three miles takes you around San Rafael Bay and into San Rafael. You can also access Sir Francis Drake Boulevard into Larkspur and pass along the Corte Madera Channel. The Richmond Bridge is a popular destination for cyclists. Only a concrete barrier wall separates riders and auto traffic.

Staff Photos HIKING WITH JON The Richmond-San Rafael Bridge path Hiking-biking trail offers 11-mile round trip from San Quentin By Jonathan Comeaux For this week’s outdoors series, we’re heading out over the water on the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge to grab some sweeping views of the Bay We start at the entrance at Tewksbury Avenue near Point Richmond and travel 5.5 miles across the Richmond Bridge to Point San Quentin, a nice 11-mile round trip. Guidelines for hiking amidst the coronavirus include: • Start with research parking or trail restrictions. Plan your route. • Be mindful. Always bring a face cover of some sort. • The earlier the better. Trails are most trafficked past noon. • No large groups. The bike and pedestrian path opened in November of 2019 and to my surprise isn’t as popular as one would imagine. On a Friday at noon, I saw just seven bikers throughout the day, meaning I would go miles without passing another person. There were no groups, and just one man with his daughter and a few fishermen hanging around Point San Quentin. The path on the Richmond Bridge is 10-feet wide, giving ample space for hikers and bikers. The trail is not as developed as the similar Bay Bridge Trail, which has a guard rail and fair amount of space separating you from traffic. On the Richmond Bridge it’s just you, concrete barriers, and cars zooming by on I-80. Going along the bridge, you’ll get increasingly better views of Point Molate and Point San Pablo toward the peak of the Richmond Bridge. You’ll also get a glimpse of the tiny Red Rock Island on your way into Marin County. My tracking device gave an elevation reading of 920 feet, but the ascent was easily manageable. This trek would be good for the beginning level hiker, child, or for cyclists working on their sprints. Continuing on the San Francisco Bay Trail for three miles takes you around San Rafael Bay and into San Rafael. You can also access Sir Francis Drake Boulevard into Larkspur and pass along the Corte Madera Channel. The trail starts on Tewksbury Avenue in Richmond and goes directly to a path to the bridge. Passing by the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge Toll Plaza. The Richmond Bridge is a popular destination for cyclists. Passing under the highest part of the Richmond Bridge. Only a concrete barrier wall separates riders and auto traffic. The trek back up the bridge will provide a nice workout.

articles.text: Maestro Michael Morgan with Oakland Symphony musicians at the November 2015 performance of the Third Symphony of Victor Bendix. Oakland Symphony is offering weekly, archival concerts featuring past performances, to be available online every Friday at 6 p.m. This week’s concert is Victor Bendix’s Symphony No. 3 in A Minor, Op. 25, originally premiered by the Symphony on November 13, 2015 at the Paramount Theatre. The selected music is from 1895. Bendix, who lived from 1851 to 1926, was the first composer played in the symphony’s “Lost Romantics” series. “Pieces from the romantic era have fallen out of the repertory for reasons that I couldn’t explain. Bendix was a Danish-Jewish composer, which could somewhat account for his music getting lost during the World War II period,” explained Maestro Michael Morgan. “This symphony is in three movements, full of melodic and harmonic inventiveness. I particularly call to your attention the second subject of the first movement about four minutes in. At that point, any doubts are cast aside and you are all in,” Morgan said. You can listen to this week’s archival concert at: https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/repast/.

San Francisco Opera is offering “Opera Aficionado”, an educational, interactive lecture series that gives opera-goers around the world front-row seats to scholarly discussions. The theme on Sunday, August 2, at 1 p.m. is “Social Themes in Opera: Past and Present,” and the first lecture series of the month will focus on operas about liberation. The guest speaker is Dramaturg Emeritus of San Francisco Opera, Dr. Clifford “Kip” Cranna. Cranna has served on the staff for 40 years and was Director of Music Administration for over 30 years. In 2008, he was awarded the San Francisco Opera Medal, the company’s highest honor, and in 2012 he received the Bernard Osher Cultural Award. The lecture will focus on ideas about liberty and freedom from oppression that have inspired opera composers through the centuries. Cranna will take viewers on a video journey, exploring the many varied ways that operas have expressed in drama and song the basic human aspiration of freedom. To register, visit https://sfopera.com/discover-opera/education/community-programs/ aficionado/. GET UP TO

articles.text: Pianist Eric Zivian The Valley of the Moon Music Festival, which this year is online, will conclude its series of concerts this Sunday, August 2. You can tune in at 4 p.m. every Saturday and Sunday, through August 2 for a total of six concerts. Patrons can livechat on YouTube with musicians and lecturers during the concert, and join afterwards for a Zoom reception. If you miss the 4 p.m. livestream, you can still watch videos of the virtual festival, made available on valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org. Saturday, August 1 will feature Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 24 in F-sharp major, Op. 78 (a Therese), and Cello Sonata No.2 in G minor, Op. 5, No. 2. Musicians featured on Saturday include festival founders Tanya Tomkins (cello) and Eric Zivian (piano), and guest artist, pianist Audrey Vardanega, founder of Musaics By the Bay in San Francisco. The closing concert, on Sunday, will feature Beethoven’s Violin Sonata No. 4 in A minor, Op. 23, and Piano Trio in E-flat major, Op.70, No.2. Sunday’s featured musicians include Francisco Fullana (violin), Tomkins, Zivian and Vardanega. Cellist Tanya Tomkins Bob Taylor, of Sonoma TV, filmed the July 19 and 25 concerts in the restored ruins of Issac DeTurk’s 1863 winery at Yulupa Ranch in Bennett Valley. Sonoma TV will also be re-broadcasting the Valley of the Moon Music Festival, with a schedule to be announced soon. Festival musicians and scholars in the festival’s Blattner Lecture Series will introduce each concert and provide commentary. Speakers include Nicholas Mathew, author of Political Beethoven and associate professor in the Department of Music at UC Berkeley, Nicholas McGegan, former Artistic Director at Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra, and Kate van Orden, Harvard University’s Dwight P. Robinson, Jr. Professor of Music. “Conversations with Kate” will be repeated at 3 p.m. on August 2, in which van Orden leads a fascinating conversation with musicologists and cellist Elaine Fitz Gibbon, about Mauricio Kagel’s film Ludwig van: A Report. All musicians originally contracted for the 2020 festival have received 50 percent of their fee. The most recent director to release a playlist is Chorus Director Dr. Lynne Morrow. Morrow became Director of the Oakland Symphony Chorus in 2005. During her tenure the scope of the Chorus has expanded to include contemporary, international, and neglected works, along with traditional choral repertoire. She conducts the Chorus’ workshop performances of major works; hosts summer choral outreach “Sing-ins;” and prepares the Chorus for work with Oakland Symphony. “I have sung or conducted all of this music. The characters are always searching, deeply within, or out into the universe. The text is always clearly sung and intentional,” Morrow said. articles.text: Melanie Laurent and Ewan McGregor star in Beginners. Movie review by Chris Honoré There is a line in Beginners, spoken by Oliver (Ewan McGregor), thirty-something, reflecting on the recent death of his father, Hal (Christopher Plummer): “My personality was created by someone else and all I got was this stupid T-shirt.” And therein is the essence of this wonderfully insightful, poignant and uplifting film. Any attempt to sort out our personalities, such as they are, and the connection to our families of our values and quirks and subtle dysfunctions, is likely a lifelong endeavor. In a sense we all get a T-shirt, at some point, worn with joy and resentment and surrendering delight. Everything about families is like a Chinese puzzle, that tube into which you stick your forefingers, one at each end, and when you begin to pull them out, the tube tightens, failing to release. To be free, if freedom is the goal, then you must do what is contraindicated. Oliver has recently lost his mother, Georgia (Mary Page Keller), to cancer. Months after her death, Hal decides, with flair and abandon, to declare that he is gay and always has been, a fact that catches Oliver completely by surprise. He had always assumed his parents loved each other but just weren’t in love. Hal’s new life inspires him, and he embraces fully his honesty and his new friends, to include a younger lover, Andy (Goren Visnjic). Hal says to Oliver, with kindness and conviction, when questioned about his coming out, “I don’t want to be theoretically gay.” From a distance, Oliver watches in wonder and amazement, leavened with love. But then, this is a film about love, about elusive, contradictory, ever-present affection, about old baggage that is packed and unpacked through a series of insightful flashbacks, beginning when Oliver’s parents marry in the 1950s. The backstory is conveyed seamlessly using old photographs and small vignettes that are filled with humor both winsome and mysterious. But then Beginners is replete with riptides of emotions, never framed by resentment or anger, but by a will to understand and accept – and always touched by regret. But then regret is an emotion that can stalk us like a dim shadow, a reminder of what could have been. Oliver’s understanding of love, as wondrous and harrowing as it can be, is challenged when, at a costume party, he meets Anna (Melanie Laurent), a lovely, enigmatic young French actress. Not only is this a love story about father and son, but about two newly met people, in their own way a bit damaged, both moving inextricably toward one another. Beginners is astonishingly well cast and acted. Christopher Plummer, as Hal, is a treasure. And Ewan McGregor, who carries the film’s point of view, is perfect. As is Melanie Laurent. All deliver understated but emotive performances that take the film to its poignant and hopeful conclusion. As an aside, Hal’s Jack Russell terrier, Arthur, who is telepathic (don’t ask, but know that it works, with subtitles, and is delightful), chews up every scene that he’s in. Beginners. Starring Ewan McGregor, Christopher Plummer, Melanie Laurent, Goren Visnjic and Mary Page Keller. Written and directed by Mike Mills. Rated R. Originally printed in the Post on July 13, 2011. Christopher Plummer and Ewan McGregor in a scene from Beginners.
articles.title: Beginners a lovely film about love

articles.text: Spielberg directs, Coen brothers write a winning film Movie review by Chris Honoré In retrospect, the Soviet Union and the United States managed to navigate almost 50 years of adversarial encounters without a confrontation that would have taken us past the brink of the deterrence known as mutual assured destruction (aka MAD). Part of the kabuki dance that the two superpowers engaged in, however, was elaborate and sustained spying. Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies, is a taut, well-made film based on a true story. It begins in 1957 with the arrest by the FBI of a Soviet spy, Rudolf Abel (Mark Ryance). The government, certain it has overwhelming evidence of his clandestine activity, decides to put him on trial. James Donovan (Tom Hanks), an insurance attorney, is selected to defend Abel who has stoically resisted all attempts by the CIA to extract information from him. What the government does not anticipate is that Donovan decides to mount a rigorous defense on Abel’s behalf, followed by an appeal of his conviction. Donovan is denigrated for carrying out what he felt was his constitutional obligation. He also suggests to the trial judge that Abel not be given the death penalty, arguing that should one of our spies be captured, we just might need Abel should there be a proffered swap. And that’s the protracted set streets are awash in institutional blues and grays. Donovan, suffering from a tenacious cold, walks ever closer to a precipice, lost in a world of duplicity and obscure signals. Movie review by Chris Honoré There is a line in Beginners, spoken by Oliver (Ewan McGregor), thirty-something, reflecting on the recent death of his father, Hal (Christopher Plummer): “My personality was created by someone else and all I got was this stupid T-shirt.” And therein is the essence of this wonderfully insightful, poignant and uplifting film. Any attempt to sort out our personalities, such as they are, and the connection to our families of our values and quirks and subtle dysfunctions, is likely a lifelong endeavor. In a sense we all get a T-shirt, at some point, worn with joy and resentment and surrendering delight. Everything about families is like a Chinese puzzle, that tube into which you stick your forefingers, one at each end, and when you begin to pull them out, the tube tightens, failing to release. To be free, if freedom is the goal, then you must do what is contraindicated. Oliver has recently lost his mother, Georgia (Mary Page Keller), to cancer. Months after her death, Hal decides, with flair and abandon, to declare that he is gay and always has been, a fact that catches Oliver completely by surprise. He had always assumed his parents loved each other but just weren’t in love. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré A Monster Calls is extraordinary and a heartfelt surprise. But take seriously its rating of PG-¡3. While the trailer seems to promise a child’s tale, involving an enormous monster in the humanoid shape of a gnarly yew tree, this British film is so much more. There is not a hint of Disney to be found, and the narrative goes far beyond the familiar palliative, “happily ever after.” At the film’s center is 12-yearold Conor (Lewis MacDougall) who is in a place in his young life that is almost more than he can bear. He is relentlessly bullied at school, haunted by a traumatic nightmare that causes him to wake in the deep of night, and coping with the life-threatening cancer that is consuming his mother (Felicity Jones). He is also unable to turn to his rigid and distant grandmother (Sigourney Weaver). His father (Toby Kebbell) has been, for most of his life, absent, living in America and though he arrives briefly due to his ex-wife’s illness, he offers little comfort to Conor. And then one night, as he sits in his room sketching in his notebook, strange things begin to happen, a pencil rolls across his desk, onto the floor. Things begin to move. And then, there, outside his opened window, stands a monster (the voice of Liam Neeson), a giant man-tree, who suddenly crashes into Conor’s room and speaks to him. He tells the boy that he will return and tell him three stories. Conor is both terrified and combative, wanting to believe yet boldly resistant to what cannot be. And so, just after midnight, the monster appears to share with Conor a fable that is gorgeously animated in watercolors (which are thematic throughout the film). The stories are puzzling, seemingly unrelated, and at first beyond Conor’s comprehension. And, as the monster points out, each is contradictory; they are not what they seem. Meanwhile, Conor goes to school and deals with the bullies and attempts to cope with the reality that his mother is slipping away from him and there is nothing he can do. Together the two of them cling to hope: his, that she will live and that each new treatment will be a cure; hers, that she can prepare her son for his life without her. Deeply conflicted, he rages against the punishment inflicted by his mother’s cancer, his anger uncontrollable, his helplessness ever with him. A Monster Calls is both a children’s allegory and an adult story. It is beautiful in its photography and in its narrative, and it never backs away from the issues that young Conor is confronting. While it could have dropped into a well of melodrama, instead it grasps life and looks at both the darkness and light and searches for a truth that is often absent from such stories. Tangentially, the monster demands that Connor tell him a fourth story that must be his own, one that the boy has refused to tell even himself. It is his deepest truth. The film, based on an idea offered by children’s author Siobhan Dowd just before she died, is realized in the 2011 award-winning book of the same title written by Patrick Ness. Conor is more a kid than an adult, and yet he stands at an intersection that asks him to be both. And both is what A Monster Calls is all about. A Monster Calls. Starring Lewis MacDougall, Felicity Jones and the voice of Liam Neeson. Directed by J.A. Bayona. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Originally printed in the Post on January 11, 2017.
articles.title: A Monster Calls – a beautiful children’s allegory from England

articles.text: French-Romany guitarist Django Reinhardt who overcame an injury to his hand early in life to create what is now known as gypsy jazz. The news media is full of stories of “Bad Guys”. With the exception of the Piedmont Post, they all tell us “that’s what sells the news”. These days, we need as much inspiration as we can get. The annals of history are loaded with the names of “Tough Guys”. Let’s forget those who push women around and pick on puny guys. Let’s take a look at those who turn adversity into victory. Our first example is violin virtuoso Maud Powell (1867- 1920). Why? First, she was a woman. Sure, history acclaims the cigar-chomping, pants-wearing George Sand; she who flung society’s norms in their faces. But Maude Powell came from a very cultured American family. The most damning thing about her was that she was American, something that was a huge impediment. at the time. The bias against American musicians was what we used to refer to as “an international conspiracy”. But she became America’s first great violinist and popular with the masses, I might add. At the opposite side of the spectrum was Ray Charles. Blindness was only one of his obstacles. And what a success he was. Crossing racial, societal and musical barriers, he earnied entry into the musical pantheon. Next, we need to mention three one-armed pianists. Count Geza Zichy (1849-1924) is the first on record. He was a Hungarian nobleman who lost his right hand in a hunting accident. Undaunted, he established himself as one of the most important pianists of the 19th century. He inspired composers to write lefthand pieces for him. So did another nobleman, Paul von Wittgenstein (1887- 1961). He was already an established concert pianist when drafted into the Austrian army in WWI. His right arm was shot off and he was imprisoned in Siberia. Also undeterred, he re-established his career and commissionied a whole library of left-hand compositions. Ravel’s piano concerto for the left hand is a famous example. These days, we are thankful for the one-handed pianist Nicholas McCarthy. Unlike those other pianists, McCarthy was born without a right hand, but chose to pursue a career as a pianist. Look him up. He is an inspiration. Michael Tilson Thomas is also noteworthy for his toughness. I was with him backstage before a concert. He fell down and broke his right wrist. I pushed him onto the stage where he played a brilliant concert at the piano. That’s toughness. Jazz guitarist Django Reinhardt also overcame a disfiguring injury. The son of a gypsy family in Romany, he suffered severe burns in a fire at the gypsy camp and lost the use of two fingers. Again, undeterred, he firecely pursued his love of playing the guitar and became world famous for his “three-fingered-lightning” and his merging of Slavic and jazz harmonics. Austrian violinist Rudolf Kolisch (1896-1978) overcame a childhood injury to his left hand, and learned to play the violin as a lefty. And now we have the international catastrophe of the coronavirus. Many segments of society are coming unglued. At the same time, many people have found ways to make considerable advancement. Viennese violinist Thomas Christian was in the hospital undergoing foot surgery. While hospitalized he still managed to practice his violin 6 to 7 hours every day. Somehow he also found time to compose cadenzas for the Beethoven violin concerto. And Hungarian violinist Antal Zalai continues to put up more videos than any violinist I can think of. So, as you can see, we have choices. We can find every excuse under the sun or use the time to our best advantage. The decision is ours.
articles.title: Overcoming adversity: Where do we go from here?

articles.text: About six years ago I was on a wine trip to the Rhone River region of France. My friend Terry Hershey and I had several appointments each day at wineries to taste the wines and write up notes for the article I would be completing back home. The wine tasting experience in France is very different than what has developed here in California. You need to have an appointment, they never charge money, they will pour every wine they make and talk endlessly about them and show you every tank and barrel. We planned on (and needed) a couple of hours per winery. They treated us as honored guests. (This is true even if you are not a wine writer. It is the appointment that does the trick.) Except on Sunday. Disregard everything I wrote above if it is a Sunday. On Sunday you are supposed to be having a 4-hour lunch with your family and drinking wine. If you own a business and it is open, there is something wrong with you. (Except the boulangeries, which are open till noon.) So, on a Sunday afternoon in January, Terry and I were driving the small scenic roads between Chateauneuf du Pape and Gigondas, admiring the nearby jagged toothlike mountains called the Dentelles du Montmirail. We come across a sign for a winery called Notre Dame des Pallieres to which was attached a small sign saying “Ouvert” (open). What? You’re kidding! We headed down the dirt driveway and discovered a charming, small winery that was indeed… open. The owner, Claude Roux, greeted us and began a generous tasting of all 12 or so of his wines. Then came some earlier vintages for comparison and to see how they age. I asked if the wines were available in the U.S. “Yes,” he said. “We have an importer based in a town in California called Richmond.” “Wow, that’s next door to the town I live in,” I told him. And thus began my introduction to wine importer Grape Expectations in Richmond. When I got home I got acquainted with Grape Expectations founder Mike Apple and started exploring their portfolio. They import wines from almost everywhere – South America, Australia and New Zealand, Spain and Italy – but it was their French portfolio that intrigued me. They have hand-selected small, high quality growers in Languedoc, Provence, Rhone Valley, Loire Valley, Burgundy, Bordeaux and Alsace – previously overlooked, and have brought them to the U.S. market.

articles.text: • The American Red Cross strongly urges healthy, eligible individuals who are feeling well to give blood or platelets to help maintain a sufficient blood supply and prevent shortages as concerns about the outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019, or COVID-19, rise in the U.S. Cold and f lu season has already impacted the nation’s ability to maintain its blood supply. As the number of coronavirus cases grows in the U.S., the number of people eligible to give blood for patients in need could decrease further. “We’re asking people to help keep the blood supply stable during this challenging time. As communities across the country prepare for this public health emergency, it’s critical that plans include a readily available blood supply for hospital patients,” said Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Blood Services. “As fears of coronavirus rise, low donor participation could harm blood availability at hospitals, and the last thing a patient should worry about is whether lifesaving blood will be on the shelf when they need it most.” Make an appointment to donate blood now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or calling the Oakland Blood Donation Center, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 510-658-6456. Donating blood is a safe process and people should not hesitate to give or receive blood. There are no data or evidence that this coronavirus can be transmissible by blood transfusion, and there have been no reported cases worldwide of transmissions for any respiratory virus, including this coronavirus, from a transfusion. The Red Cross only collects blood from individuals who are healthy and feeling well at the time of donation – and who meet other eligibility requirements, available at RedCrossBlood.org. At each blood drive and donation center, Red Cross employees follow thorough safety protocols including wearing gloves, routinely wiping down donortouched areas, using sterile collection sets for every donation, and preparing the arm for donation with an aseptic scrub. These mitigation measures will help ensure blood recipient safety, as well as staff and donor safety in reducing contact with those who may potentially have this respiratory infection. The Red Cross has implemented new blood donation deferrals out of an abundance of caution. Individuals are asked to postpone their donation for 28 days following: • Travel to China and its special administrative regions, Hong Kong and Macau, as well as Iran, Italy and South Korea; Diagnosis of COVID-19, contact with a person who has or is suspected to have the virus. As the situation evolves, the Red Cross will continue to evaluate all emerging risks in collaboration with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and industry partners to determine if additional intervention strategies are needed. Together, we stand ready to keep the American public informed and prepared. Blood donation process A blood donation takes about an hour from start to finish, but the actual donation itself only takes about 8-10 minutes. Donors can also save up to 15 minutes at the blood drive by completing a RapidPass®. With RapidPass®, donors complete the pre-donation reading and health history questionnaire online, on the day of donation, from a mobile device or computer. To complete a RapidPass®, follow the instructions at RedCrossBlood.org/RapidPass or use the Red Cross Blood Donor App. To donate blood, individuals need to bring a blood donor card or driver’s license or two other forms of identification that are required at check-in. Individuals who are 17 years of age in most states (16 with parental consent where allowed by state law), weigh at least 110 pounds and are in generally good health may be eligible to donate blood. High school students and other donors 18 years of age and younger also must meet certain height and weight requirements. Oakland Blood Donation Center, 6230 Claremont Avenue. articles.text: Terry Smith is a gardener with a mission. “Mine is a habitat garden. Nearly everything that grows here has a purpose to feed, nurture or shelter creatures, human or otherwise,” says Smith, a former Havens Elementary School science teacher, co-founder of Piedmont Connect (www.piedmontconnect.org) and cofounder of the Pollinator Posse (www.pollinatorposse.org). Since Smith and her husband bought home at Jerome and Oakland Avenue 38 years ago, they have transformed both front and back yards from lawn and eucalyptus trees to native and/or drought-tolerant plants, pollinator habitat and edibles. Their front garden is now an orchard underplanted with pollinator-friendly plants and designated an official Monarch Butterfly Waystation. The backyard features raised vegetable beds surrounded by fruit trees, a water feature, seating areas and more host plants. Many of the 27 fruit trees are multi-grafted to produce different varieties from the same trees. “By planting year-round and preserving the bounty, I can eat something from the garden every day of the year,” Smith says. “I freeze, can, dehydrate and share any extra. We’re so lucky with our climate here that the garden is often more productive in the winter months than a typical summer harvest.” Smith’s gardening strategies Water conservation: “Water is efficiently applied only as needed. I recently learned that homegrown vegetables and fruit use 1/30th the water of those raised commercially. Our water use is far less than when the garden was lawn, but the land is far Photo by Rob Smith Terry Smith’s Pollinator Posse creation of super-sized, silk Monarch Butterflies and caterpillars won the “Most Artistic” award in Piedmont’s 2020 Fourth of July “Celebrate in Place” competition. She created the giant butterflies originally for the 2019 Autumn Festival of Lights at Lake Merritt. more productive.” Toxin free: “No pesticides or herbicides ever, and plants are purchased from carefully vetted nurseries, or grown from seed to avoid those treated with neonicotinoids. Neonics are systemic poisons that render a plant toxic throughout its life cycle. Most wholesale growers apply these to plants and often don’t inform the nurseries that buy them. Even more disturbing is the use of these systemic, addictive and toxic chemicals on many food crops. Diverse habitat to nurture pollinators: “I choose many plants for their affiliation with wildlife, especially pollinators. The incredible decline in recent years of insect populations — the base of our food chain — is primarily the result of pesticides and climate change.” “The benefit of providing habitat and sustenance for these creatures includes a high yield of fruits and vegetables – nothing goes unpollinated – and their pleasant company. Since butterflies in particular need specific plants to complete their life cycles – caterpillars are the original picky eaters – I make sure I have as many of those plants as possible.” Climate Corner is a collaboration between the city of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect, a local environmental nonprofit, to raise awareness about climate actions in the community.
