articles.text: J. Harper Gaston M.D. died on July 12, 2020 in Atlanta, Georgia due to complications of dementia. He was 88. Dr. Gaston was a most caring father and grandfather, a loving husband of sixty-seven years, and an honorable, dedicated, and talented physician, who was beloved by his many patients, family, and friends. He worked for the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group of Northern California for over 20 years, and later founded and served as the first Medical Director and Physician-in-Chief of the Kaiser Permanente Southeastern Medical Group in Atlanta, Georgia. Born J. Harper Gaston IV on November 2, 1931 in New York City, he was the son of Joseph H. Gaston III M.D and Louese Hays Gaston. Raised in Columbus, Georgia, where his father practiced orthopedic medicine, Harper Gaston attended city schools in Columbus and graduated from the Darlington School in Rome, Georgia. After his father’s death, Dr. Gaston worked as a grocery clerk to help support his mother and to earn his tuition money. At age 16, he entered Emory University, where he received both his Bachelor (1952) and Medical Degree (1955). While attending Emory Medical School, he met and married the love of his life, his medical school classmate, Dr. Anne Elizabeth Hendrick. Both doctors completed their internships and residencies at Grady Memorial Hospital. He was named the first fellow in Cardiology under the direction of world-renown cardiologist, Dr. J. Willis Hurst. Upon completion of his residency program, Dr. Gaston enlisted in the U.S. Air Force and was stationed at Kessler Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi. With the rank of Capt., he served as a general internist and (oddly) Chair of the Dermatology department while his wife, Dr. Anne Gaston worked as a civilian pediatrician in the Kessler Air Force Base General Hospital. In 1961 he and his wife moved first to Oakland, and then to Piedmont, where they joined the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group in the KPMG’s first medical office in San Leandro. Their decision of the home games in the World Series from 1972-1974. In Atlanta, Dr. Gaston continued his community service, by serving the Emory University Medical School in many capacities for over 50 years, including as an adviser to the Emory University System of Healthcare Board of Directors, as a member of the Emory Board of Visitors, and as Co-Chair with his wife of the National Council of Medicine. The Drs. Gaston also established the Gaston Service Scholarships for Emory University Medical School students who exemplified community volunteerism and service. “Service in and of itself is the greatest reward that our profession can offer us. It is the heart of medicine,” he said. He was awarded the Emory Medal in 1997, Emory’s Highest Honor, for his service to Emory and the community. Dr. Gaston remained an avid sports fan of the Oakland A’s, the Oakland Raiders, the Atlanta Braves, and the Georgia “Dawgs” for all of his life. He loved to travel and traveled with one of the first groups of physicians to visit the USSR in the late 1960s. He also loved horse racing and was a co-owner of Dogwood Stables in Aiken, South Carolina. His one disappointment in life was when Dogwood’s horse, Summer Squall, won the 1990 Preakness, but despite being the favorite to win, came in second in the 1990 Kentucky Derby. His greatest achievement was his generosity of spirit and his tremendous love for his wife and family. Dr. J. Harper Gaston is survived by his wife, Dr. Anne Elizabeth Hendrick Gaston, his only child, Lisa Anne Gaston, his sonin-law Michael Gerard Reff, and his two granddaughters and their spouses, Allison Elizabeth Stalla (Timothy Zeid Stalla) and Hayley Harper Swarbrick (Andrew John Swarbrick). A private service will be held at Greenville Presbyterian Church Cemetery, where Dr. Harper Gaston will be laid to rest. A public memorial service will be planned and announced at a later date. articles.text: Richard “Dick” Brooks passed away peacefully at age 92 on July 18, 2020 at the Terraces in Boise, Idaho. He was a 22-year resident of Piedmont through 1987, and long-time resident of Ketchum, Idaho. Born in 1928 in Akron, Ohio, Dick marked his life in Milwaukee, Yale University, Dallas, and San Francisco, then Piedmont before retiring to Ketchum. Linguistically precise and athletically adept, Dick spent his career in finance and was the architect of one of the first interest-rate currency swaps, recognized in 1983 as “the most noteworthy financial swap” by Institutional Investor magazine. Outside of work, he had a penchant for the precise: the structure of a sonnet, the turn of a phrase, the fine cut of woodworking. Known to many family members as “Squeak”, he was a loving dad and grandfather who taught his family what it was to be respected and respectful. He loved song and was an orator of notable skill. His voice will live on in our hearts as we focus on being aware of life’s moments, often with ice cream and/or Scotch. During his time in Piedmont, he was a member of the executive council of the Boy Scout Council in the 1970s, and helped to maintain the independence of the Piedmont Council, which continues to this day. Dick is survived by his wife Sidney, and his children Dave (wife Ann, daughter Jennings), Scott (wife Emily, sons Alexander, Zachary, and Mitchell), and Susie (husband Patrick, daughters Katie and Sammie). A memorial service will be held on August 7 at St. Thomas Episcopal Church in Sun Valley, Idaho, where he will be laid to rest in the columbarium. Dick Brooks, who lived in Piedmont from 1965 through 1987, passed away on July 18, 2020 in Boise Idaho. Je was 92.

articles.text: Two residents of The Lake Merritt enjoy a stroll at the lake. There aren’t many major cities where you can drive from the grocery store to the middle of a redwood forest in five or 10 minutes/ A little secret is that you can in Oakland. Residents of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living have been exploring our wonderful local parks in a safe and distanced way. The City of Oakland boasts nearly 6,000 acres of parks and trails, many of which connect to larger park networks. The East Bay Regional Parks features nearly 125,000 acres and has a very good website that is continuously updated with COVID-related closures and other information. We also use alltrails.com to search for easy hikes, and read user reviews about trail width and busyness. Locally, you can walk for days without retracing your steps. Recently, our residents enjoyed a great presentation by Stan Dodson, the founder of Oakland Trails (oaklandtrails.org), as part of our weekly public speaker series, “Topics of Merritt.” This and our other Zoom programs are free and available to the public, so call us or register online. Dodson is a person who knows his local trails. He is a recipient of the Parkland Steward Award from Oakland Public Works Department, and the Anne Woodell Community Award, Oakland’s highest honor for community service in parks. Dodson recommends visiting Oakland’s gorgeous parks in the afternoon on weekdays to avoid crowds. He also recommended to our audience some easy and accessible trails within the Oakland City Parks system. On the Eastern side of Joaquin Miller Park there is a nearly flat maintenance road that can be accessed from a parking pullout on Skyline Boulevard near the Big Trees Trailhead. This road takes you through the redwood forest toward the Sequoia Horse Arena in Roberts Park. This trail is wheelchair accessible and peaceful. Within the nearby Sausal Creek watershed, Dodson recommends entering the Dimond Canyon Trail at El Centro Avenue in the Glenview District. There you will find a flat, wide trail that attracts families and is suitable for nearly all abilities. In addition to these spots, The Lake Merritt residents have several favorites to share. articles.text: We often talk of “meaningful” engagement or activity as if there is just one type of meaning. The truth is that what is meaningful to one person may not be so to another, especially when that person needs assistance with activities of daily living. When something is meaningless, it lacks purpose, value or significance. Certainly no one is striving to spend their time in a meaningless way, and yet maintaining boring routines can feel futile to people. There can be a lack of joy or inspiration when people are stuck in a rut of meaningless activity. Here are some examples of meaningless activities: • Checking email just because • Scrolling through social media feeds • Viewing TV alone or watching the same programs repeatedly Conversely, when something is meaningful it is “full of significance” and has purpose. When caring for someone who might need elder care due to age or chronic conditions that have altered their physical abilities, it is important to find ways to spend time together that is worthwhile to them. Here are some examples of meaningful activities: • Gardening can be meaningful if it brings someone the joy of growing their own food or waiting for the flowers to bloom. This also can engage all of one’s senses, which tends to increase the meaning of an activity. • Making a photo album for sharing memories with someone in your life. It can be to give as a gift or have as a keepsake. • Listening to music which can evoke memories to be shared or be part of creating new ones. In order to find out what is meaningful to another person who needs your help, you might ask what they love to do or what they are good at. Even if they physically cannot do it alone, maybe you can assist so they still have the feeling of engaging in this activity. Remember that one person may find coloring in pictures to be relaxing and rewarding while someone else might think it is mind-numbing and pointless. Creating a shared activity in which people need to talk or rely on one another to complete a larger task can be meaningful, so it is not just about one or two people. Think of a letter-writing campaign or making a meal together for group activities. For more ideas on how to create meaningful activities visit the Changing Aging blog at changingaging.org. Dear MacMama: I just got a MacBook Pro, and since I am not going into work, I have time to learn how to use it. I am coming from the PC world, so everything is different. Where do I start? -Leslie G., Oakland Dear Leslie: Congrats on your new purchase, and luckily, there are many good sources that provide information on becoming comfortable on the Mac platform. You can find help with books, online print sources, and videos. Here are some of my favorite sources. Books: I am still a page turning learner, and if I am learning something new, I like to sit with a highlighter and a book, and study like the old days! There are some excellent books on switching to Mac, whether you are a tech savvy user, or more of a beginner. The “For Dummies” series is excellent, and there is a “Switching to a Mac for Dummies”. Anything by David Pogue is great, although a bit more technical. One that I would strongly recommend is “macOS Catalina for Dummies” by Bob LeVitus. Also, the “for seniors” volumes are usually well written, specifically Mac OS Catalina for Seniors” by Scott La Counte. Be aware, that if these volumes are not current (2019 or later), the info might be outdated. Websites: Apple itself has a web page devoted to folks who switched to Mac from PCs: https://support. apple.com/en-us/HT204216 You can find lots of good info here. I also really like the “How to Geek”: https://www.howtogeek. com/437168/how-to-switch-froma-windows-pc-to-a-mac/. Another good source is wired. com. If you do a Google search “switching from PC to Mac” there are countless links from established sites. Videos (YouTube): This is most likely your best bet. Anson Alexander has really good video series and his Mac tutorial for beginners is excellent: https://www.youtube.com/ Another good video is by macmost.com, including a video on “Questions New Mac Owners Have When Switching from Windows”: https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=vau_4NpkEB8. Of course, there are plenty of videos by helpful pros, and if you just got a new mac, you can always call AppleCare with any questions: 1-800-275-2273. I think you will find that there are many similarities, and the differences are mostly for power users. Of course, the file structure is different, and the user experience is also a bit different. If you are a photographer, artist or musician, you will appreciate the amount of software for you. And these days, the current version of Microsoft Office apps like Word and Excel are almost exactly the same on the Mac as PC. I would say, that within a month or so, you will feel like a pro. If you need more guidance, contact me, I am doing all of my support appointments remotely these days. articles.text: Barbara Addleman and sons Blaise and Kleed Cumming were awarded the Highland Saucer this week for the “Most Patriotic” entry in the Piedmont Fourth of July Front Yard Decorating Contest. In the absence of a parade this year – the first in the parade’s 55-year history – the Fourth of July Committee invited the community to compete in a “celebrating in place” contest. The Addleman-Cumming family transformed their yard into a history of civil protests in the U.S., replete with 23 cardboard protest signs, and 40 additional signs in a bay window. On the front of the house was a large “Power to the People” banner. Their entry, called “This is What Democracy Looks Like,” was sparked by the Black Lives Matter demonstrations and the family’s keen awareness of social issues. “We have always been active politically and socially by joining demonstrations for the women’s march or against Monsanto and climate change,” Addleman said. Signs at their house included a range of statements, including “Google Fred Hampton,” “Who Watches the Watchers,” “Water is Life,” ”Medicare for All,” and “Freedom of the Press.” Kleed Cummings explained Barbara Addleman’s front yard filled with signs representing an entry in the 4th of July Yard Decorating contest titled, “This is What Democracy Looks Like.” Carla Betts, Chair of the July Fourth Parade committee, presents the Highland Saucer to Kleed Cumming (left)and brother Blaise, and their mother Barbara Addleman for the “Most Patriotic” entry into Piedmont’s first ever Fourth of July “Front Yard and Car Decorating Contest.” the importance of their project, “Piedmont is definitely an affluent town that is pretty privileged and might not necessarily be acknowledging these social movements going on right now. We just thought it would be good to highlight them for everyone.” “Demonstrating is ingrained in being patriotic and being American,” his mother added. “It goes back to the Boston Tea Party. People going out, demonstrating, and participating in democracy is part of why we have all the things that we do have.” The three started planning out their July 4 entry a week ahead of time and spent three long, but fun, afternoons in the yard making the signs from recycled material. Their hard work paid off, Addleman admitted. “I was totally surprised when I got the call from Carla Betts. We sort of said, ‘oh well, we haven’t heard from them, but it was fun to do.’ But then we got the call and we said, “Oh my god, they actually called!” Piedmonters can still check out their award-winning front yard on Carmel Avenue. When thinking of taking their installment down recently, the Cumming-Addleman family decided to leave something out there. “If nothing else, just to continue it will support the people in Portland,” she said.

articles.text: Over the weekend of July 18, graffiti with anti-police messages popped up at two locations in Piedmont. With graffiti a hot topic nationwide, especially in Portland and Oakland, Piedmont has discovered it is not immune. At the Hall Fenway, which connects Wildwood and Crocker Avenue, a bench, street sign and the sidewalk were tagged. The messages included “ACAB,” anti-police sentiment and a message about “one percent.” On Guilford and Highland similar messages, with the same color spray paint, targeted the sidewalk and a street sign. According to California penal code 594, “If the amount of defacement, damage, or destruction is four hundred dollars ($400) or more, vandalism is punishable by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by a fine of not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000).” Under $400 in damage can be punished with up to one year in county jail and up to a $1,000 fine. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers weighed in on the delicacy of the situation. “I understand the raw emotional state which comes from a number of factors, but vandalizing property isn’t going to move the needle. Constructive, purposeful engagement will,” he said. Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan has not seen much graffiti of any kind in his three years in the City, so this represented something of a first. “We had a little bit of anti-police graffiti right after George Floyd. It was nothing dramatic like in the big cities,” he explained. “There was a little chalk graffiti around the civic center. Beyond that, we have had very, very little – and hopefully will not have any.”

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, July 29, 2020 Cumming-Addleman family wins Highland Saucer By Jay Russell Barbara Addleman and sons Blaise and Kleed Cumming were awarded the Highland Saucer this week for the “Most Patriotic” entry in the Piedmont Fourth of July Front Yard Decorating Contest. In the absence of a parade this year – the first in the parade’s 55-year history – the Fourth of July Committee invited the community to compete in a “celebrating in place” contest. The Addleman-Cumming family transformed their yard into a history of civil protests in the U.S., replete with 23 cardboard protest signs, and 40 additional signs in a bay window. On the front of the house was a large “Power to the People” banner. Their entry, called “This is What Democracy Looks Like,” was sparked by the Black Lives Matter demonstrations and the family’s keen awareness of social issues. “We have always been active politically and socially by joining demonstrations for the women’s march or against Monsanto and climate change,” Addleman said. Signs at their house included a range of statements, including “Google Fred Hampton,” “Who Watches the Watchers,” “Water is Life,” ”Medicare for All,” and “Freedom of the Press.” Kleed Cummings explained Barbara Addleman’s front yard filled with signs representing an entry in the 4th of July Yard Decorating contest titled, “This is What Democracy Looks Like.” Carla Betts, Chair of the July Fourth Parade committee, presents the Highland Saucer to Kleed Cumming (left)and brother Blaise, and their mother Barbara Addleman for the “Most Patriotic” entry into Piedmont’s first ever Fourth of July “Front Yard and Car Decorating Contest.” the importance of their project, “Piedmont is definitely an affluent town that is pretty privileged and might not necessarily be acknowledging these social movements going on right now. We just thought it would be good to highlight them for everyone.” “Demonstrating is ingrained in being patriotic and being American,” his mother added. “It goes back to the Boston Tea Party. People going out, demonstrating, and participating in democracy is part of why we have all the things that we do have.” The three started planning out their July 4 entry a week ahead of time and spent three long, but fun, afternoons in the yard making the signs from recycled material. Their hard work paid off, Addleman admitted. “I was totally surprised when I got the call from Carla Betts. We sort of said, ‘oh well, we haven’t heard from them, but it was fun to do.’ But then we got the call and we said, “Oh my god, they actually called!” Piedmonters can still check out their award-winning front yard on Carmel Avenue. When thinking of taking their installment down recently, the Cumming-Addleman family decided to leave something out there. “If nothing else, just to continue it will support the people in Portland,” she said. 2020 Calendar of Events July 29 - August 19 Meetings will be conducted by ZOOM and should be viewable on KCOM (Channel 27) and on the City’s website: piedmont.ca.gov. Recreation Commission . ...............................Virtual meeting via Zoom Graffiti in Piedmont – a follow-up By Jay Russell Over the weekend of July 18, graffiti with anti-police messages popped up at two locations in Piedmont. With graffiti a hot topic nationwide, especially in Portland and Oakland, Piedmont has discovered it is not immune. At the Hall Fenway, which connects Wildwood and Crocker Avenue, a bench, street sign and the sidewalk were tagged. The messages included “ACAB,” anti-police sentiment and a message about “one percent.” On Guilford and Highland similar messages, with the same color spray paint, targeted the sidewalk and a street sign. According to California penal code 594, “If the amount of defacement, damage, or destruction is four hundred dollars ($400) or more, vandalism is punishable by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by a fine of not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000).” Under $400 in damage can be punished with up to one year in county jail and up to a $1,000 fine. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers weighed in on the delicacy of the situation. “I understand the raw emotional state which comes from a number of factors, but vandalizing property isn’t going to move the needle. Constructive, purposeful engagement will,” he said. Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan has not seen much graffiti of any kind in his three years in the City, so this represented something of a first. “We had a little bit of anti-police graffiti right after George Floyd. It was nothing dramatic like in the big cities,” he explained. “There was a little chalk graffiti around the civic center. Beyond that, we have had very, very little – and hopefully will not have any.” THIS WEEK IN HISTORY: 14 years ago: August 2, 2006 The summer of 2006 brought a life-changing journey for the Ensemble group of the Piedmont Choirs. A two-week tour of performances I the Far East gave the young vocalists an opportunity to compete in Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore. In addition to a rigorous competition schedule, the group got to see the sights and taste the flavors of the Far East while meeting other youth singers from international choral groups.
